title: Glad three times
hookLine: glad before giving, glad while giving, glad after (AN 6.37)
carry: glad before, bright during, happy after

cards: You know the kind of gift that goes wrong in the middle. You pick out a present, happy. Then you see the price tag and wince.
You wrap it, and a little voice says they'd better appreciate this. A week later you're still annoyed they never mentioned it. The gift has cost you three times: in money, in mood, and in resentment.
The Buddha once praised a gift given by a laywoman, and he described exactly what made it shine. Part of his answer was about the giver's heart, and it has three moments.

teach.b: The story is in the Numerical Discourses, book of sixes.
A laywoman named Nandamata, known for her devotion, had prepared a gift of food for the community of monks, with the Buddha's two chief disciples, Sariputta and Moggallana, at its head.
The Buddha, the text says, saw the offering from afar and told the monks that this gift had six factors.
Three belong to the ones who receive: they are free of greed, hatred and delusion, or practicing to be. And three belong to the giver. Before giving, the giver is glad.
While giving, the giver's heart is bright and confident. After giving, the giver is uplifted.

teach.h: GLAD BEFORE, BRIGHT DURING, HAPPY AFTER.
teach.b: There's a short Pali verse that people still chant about it: glad before, bright during, happy after.

teach.h: THE GLADNESS IS PART OF THE GIFT.
teach.b: The striking part is that the gladness isn't a reward that comes later. It's part of the gift itself. A gift given grudgingly, with a wince in the middle and resentment after, is still a gift, but it's thinner.
A gift given gladly all the way through, the text says, is great in fruit, beyond measuring. So the practice isn't just give more.

It's paying attention to how you give: the gladness while you choose it and picture their face, the brightness in the moment of giving, and afterward, instead of waiting for thanks, going back to enjoy it.
Recollecting your own generosity is itself a traditional meditation. You're allowed to feel good about a good thing.

how: Many Buddhists give with attention to their own state of mind, and recollecting one's past generosity (caganussati) is a traditional meditation; the verse on being glad before, during and after is still chanted.

o: a blessing chanted for the giver
the merit a gift earns later

games.q: match the moment to how the giver feels.
p: the heart is bright and confident

s: in this teaching, gladness is a reward that comes long after the gift
gladness is part of the gift itself: before, during and after.
three of the six factors belong to those who receive
they are free of greed, hatred and delusion, or practicing to be.
recollecting your own generosity is a traditional meditation
it's called caganussati, the recollection of generosity.

games.q: you gave a friend a thoughtful gift a week ago and they never mentioned it. you notice resentment creeping in. what does this teaching point to?
o: remind them, so they say thank you.
go back and enjoy the gladness of having given.
games.why: the giver's third moment is uplift after giving. it doesn't depend on thanks: you can recollect the gift and be glad.

practice: Bring to mind a gift you gave that went well: a meal, a favor, a present, an hour of help. Remember the gladness of choosing it, the brightness as it reached their hands and face, and how it felt later that day.
Let that gladness spread through the body with the breath; nothing to prove, just a good thing you did.

wordCard.voice: Sumana. Glad-minded, of good heart: the giver's part of a great gift, glad before giving, bright while giving, uplifted after.

orig.note: Pali: glad-minded, of good heart; the giver is sumana before giving.

carryVoice: Your line: glad before, bright during, happy after. The gladness is part of the gift. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 6.37 (Chalangadana Sutta), the six-factored gift
